info.name: PlatinumCoin Pix — Local
info.description:
Living collection for testing the platform locally, **organized one folder per service**.

It grows incrementally: every step that adds a public endpoint adds the request here, under its service's folder (convention in CLAUDE.md). Step 48 only finalizes it (pre-request auth, idempotency automation, richer examples).

## How to use
1. Import this file and `pix-platform.local.postman_environment.json` into Postman; select the **PlatinumCoin Pix — Local** environment.
2. Run **auth-service → Login (alice)** first — it saves `accessToken` into the environment, so every authenticated request below reuses it automatically.
3. Base URLs come from `*BaseUrl` env vars (ports mirror `docs/local-dev.md`).

CLI alternative: `newman run tools/postman/pix-platform.postman_collection.json -e tools/postman/pix-platform.local.postman_environment.json`.

item.name: auth-service
item.description: Identity service — port 8081. Login issues the HS256 JWT that every other service validates. See services/auth-service/README.md.

exec: // Save the token so every authenticated request in this collection reuses it.

request.description: Authenticate the seeded user alice (acc-001). On success, saves `accessToken` to the environment.
Authenticate the seeded user bob (acc-002). Switches `accessToken` to bob's token.
Wrong password ⇒ 401 application/problem+json (no stack trace). Demonstrates the RFC 7807 error contract.

Return the caller identity the common-lib JwtAuthFilter derived from the bearer token (`{userId, accountId}`). Run a Login request first so `{{accessToken}}` is set. Without the header it returns 401 problem+json (`code: UNAUTHORIZED`).
Actuator health — the contract compose healthchecks rely on. Expect {"status":"UP"}.

item.name: account-service
item.description: Accounts & Pix keys — port 8082. First service backed by DynamoDB. Reads pix_accounts. Run auth-service → Login first so `{{accessToken}}` is set. See services/account-service/README.md.

exec: // Money at the public edge is a decimal BRL string (e.g. "5000.00"), never a float.

request.description: The caller's own account (`{accountId, status, dailyLimit}`), derived only from the JWT `accountId` claim — no way to name another account. Login as alice vs bob to see the account track the token. Without the header ⇒ 401 problem+json (`code: UNAUTHORIZED`).

exec: // Service-to-service view keeps money as integer cents (a JSON number), not a string.

request.description: Service-to-service lookup by account id (ADR-0006). Returns integer `dailyLimitCents` for callers that do integer math on the limit. Requires a valid token but is not account-scoped (a purely internal seam). Unknown id ⇒ 404 problem+json (`code: ACCOUNT_NOT_FOUND`).

exec: // Re-running against the same value now returns 409 KEY_ALREADY_EXISTS (global uniqueness).

request.description: Register a Pix key. Global uniqueness is enforced by a conditional `PutItem` (`attribute_not_exists(pk)`) — a value already taken by any account ⇒ 409 problem+json (`code: KEY_ALREADY_EXISTS`). EMAIL is normalized (trim + lowercase); a malformed value ⇒ 422 (`code: INVALID_PIX_KEY`). For `keyType: EVP` the server mints a UUID and ignores `keyValue`. Owner comes from the JWT, never the body.

exec: // The list is scoped to the caller's JWT account — never another account's keys.

request.description: List the caller's Pix keys (GSI1 query on `ACCOUNT#<accountId from JWT>`). Returns only this account's keys.

exec: // Deleting another account's key ⇒ 403 KEY_FORBIDDEN (existence revealed on purpose);

request.description: Delete an owned Pix key ⇒ 204. Ownership-guarded: another account's key ⇒ 403 problem+json (`code: KEY_FORBIDDEN`, existence revealed since Pix keys are globally resolvable); an absent key ⇒ 404 (`code: KEY_NOT_FOUND`).

exec: // Register `alice@platinum.com` first (Register Pix key) so this resolves; an unknown
// key ⇒ 404 KEY_NOT_FOUND only when BACEN's DICT does not hold it either (step 30).

request.description:
account-service's DICT role (ADR-0006 internal seam): resolve a Pix key to its destination. An internal key ⇒ `{internal:true, accountId, keyType}` (register it first via `Register Pix key`). The local `pix_keys` table is tried **first** and BACEN's DICT is not consulted at all for a key we already hold — this is the hottest read on the send path, so it must not pay a network hop.

Since step 30 a key we do *not* hold is delegated to BACEN's DICT (see the sibling request `Resolve Pix key (external / BACEN DICT)`); `404 KEY_NOT_FOUND` now means unknown to **both** directories, and a DICT that cannot be reached answers `503 DIRECTORY_UNAVAILABLE` instead. Requires a valid token (`/internal/**` is not public); the incoming key is lowercase-normalized to mirror registration.

exec: pm.test('carries the holder ISPB and no local account', () => { pm.expect(body.externalBank).to.eql('99999999'); pm.expect(body.accountId).to.be.oneOf([null, undefined]); });

request.description:
The step-11 seam, closed in step 30. `bob@otherbank.com` is registered nowhere in PlatinumCoin, so account-service delegates the lookup to BACEN's DICT (`GET /spi/dict/{key}` on mock-bacen) and answers `{internal:false, externalBank:"99999999"}` — which is what makes the **external** send branch reachable (debit to `SPI_CLEARING`, settle asynchronously).

**Four answers, and telling them apart is the point:** held here → `{internal:true, accountId}`; held elsewhere → this response; known to **neither** directory → `404 KEY_NOT_FOUND`; and the DICT **unreachable** → `503 DIRECTORY_UNAVAILABLE` + `Retry-After`, deliberately not a 404 — telling a payer their payee's key does not exist because *our* dependency is down is a lie that also discourages the retry that would work. Try it: `docker compose stop mock-bacen-spi` and re-send.

The local table is tried **first**, so an internal key costs zero network hops — this is the hottest read on the send path.
Actuator health — the contract compose healthchecks rely on. Expect {"status":"UP"}.

exec: pm.test('Location points at the status resource', () => pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get('Location')).to.eql('/v1/payments/' + body.transactionId));

request.description:
Walking skeleton of the send flow (step 18): validate the body, mint `txId` + Pix-standard `endToEndId` (`E<ISPB><yyyyMMddHHmm-UTC><random>`), persist the transaction as `RECEIVED`, and return `202 Accepted` + `Location`.

**The debtor is the JWT, never the body** — the payload has `pixKey`, `amount`, `description` and *no* source-account field (Domain Safety Rule #1). The `Idempotency-Key` header is required by the contract; this skeleton accepts and ignores it (the claim + replay is step 19).
`"0.00"` matches the wire pattern but is not money: the strictly-positive rule (which the pattern cannot express) rejects it in the domain as a distinct `INVALID_AMOUNT`.
`"12.5"` fails the `^\d{1,9}\.\d{2}$` bean-validation pattern (one decimal), so it is a `400 VALIDATION_ERROR` before the use case runs.

item.name: Send Pix — above daily limit (422 LIMIT_EXCEEDED)

request.description: Step 20's daily-limit check (ADR-0007). The seeded daily limit is R$ 5,000.00, so a single R$ 9,000 send alone exceeds it and is refused with `422 LIMIT_EXCEEDED` **before any money moves** — no transaction is persisted. The limit is read server-side from account-service and reserved against a per-account, São-Paulo-calendar-day counter; the decision object carries the `REQUIRE_STEP_UP` MFA seam (today mapped to deny).

exec: pm.test('external status is PROCESSING (not settled yet — the money is in SPI_CLEARING)', () => pm.expect(body.status).to.eql('PROCESSING'));
pm.test('Location points at the status resource', () => pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get('Location')).to.eql('/v1/payments/' + body.transactionId));

request.description:
The **external** branch (step 27). Identical wire shape to the internal send — only the destination key differs, because authority, limits and fraud are properties of the *payer*, not of where the payee banks. `bob@otherbank.com` is registered in no PlatinumCoin account, so account-service delegates to BACEN's DICT and answers `{internal:false, externalBank:"99999999"}` (null `accountId`).

So the payer is debited and the money is parked in the internal `SPI_CLEARING` account — no ACID transaction can span two banks, and crediting a clearing account keeps double-entry symmetry (Σ balances unchanged). The transaction rests at `DEBITED` (external status `PROCESSING`), **not** `SETTLED`: only BACEN can close the gap to the other PSP.

It finishes **asynchronously** — payment-service's outbox publishes `PixDebited` → settlement-service (port 8086, step 31) long-polls `settlement-queue`, calls the mock SPI, and walks `DEBITED → SENT_TO_SPI → SETTLED`. Run this, then **Get payment status** a moment later to watch `PROCESSING` flip to `SETTLED`. Requires `settlement-service` + `mock-bacen-spi` running.

item.name: Send Pix — idempotent replay (send twice, one debit)

exec: pm.test('202 Accepted (fresh accept the first time, memoized replay after)', () => pm.response.to.have.status(202));
// Send this request a SECOND time without changing anything: the fixed Idempotency-Key
// makes it replay — same transactionId as the first run, and NO second debit.
if (seen) { pm.test('replay returns the SAME transactionId (no second transaction)', () => pm.expect(body.transactionId).to.eql(seen)); }

request.description:
The idempotency contract (step 19, ADR-0002) — invisible in every send card above because each auto-mints a fresh `Idempotency-Key` (`{{$guid}}`), so a retry always looks like a new payment. This request pins a **constant** `Idempotency-Key`, so sending it twice proves the guarantee.

**First send:** a new payment is accepted — `202`, a fresh `txId`, money moves once. **Every later send:** the memoized `202` is replayed — the *same* `transactionId`/`endToEndId`, and **no** second debit (the test asserts the id is unchanged). That is layer 1 of ADR-0002: a claim/replay lifecycle keyed by `(accountId, Idempotency-Key)`.

Keep the key but change the `amount` → `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED` (same key, different body is a conflict, not a replay). Omit the header entirely → `400 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED`. The memo is durable (DynamoDB, 24h TTL), so the replay survives a process crash between the two sends.

exec: pm.test('external status is one of the wire vocabulary', () => pm.expect(['PROCESSING','SETTLED','FAILED','REVERSED','REJECTED']).to.include(body.status));
pm.test('an internal send is already SETTLED', () => pm.expect(body.status).to.eql('SETTLED'));

request.description:
Owner-only status query (step 22). Run **Send Pix — alice → bob (202)** first: it captures `paymentTxId`, and this card polls `GET /v1/payments/{id}` for it.

The response is the external view of the internal state machine — clients see `PROCESSING / SETTLED / FAILED / REVERSED / REJECTED`, never internal names like `DEBITED`, so the machine can evolve without breaking mobile clients. An **internal** send has already settled (the atomic ledger posting *is* the settlement), so it reads back `SETTLED` with `settledAt` — even though the `202` said `PROCESSING`.

Ownership is enforced from the JWT: a token for another account, or an unknown id, both return `404 PAYMENT_NOT_FOUND` (never `403`) so existence never leaks.

item.name: Get payment status — someone else's / unknown (404)

request.description: An unknown transaction id — and, identically, another account's real id — returns `404 PAYMENT_NOT_FOUND`. The two cases are deliberately indistinguishable: a `403` would confirm a foreign id is real and let a caller enumerate other accounts' transactions (Domain Safety Rule #1 — existence must not leak).
Liveness/readiness surface the compose healthcheck probes.

item.name: settlement-service
item.description:
The SPI connector, in **both directions** — port 8086. Its outbound half is queue-driven and has no HTTP surface at all (send an external Pix and watch it reach `SETTLED`; there is nothing to click here for it). Its **inbound** half, step 37, is this webhook: the route BACEN calls to deliver a Pix to one of our customers.

**JWT-exempt, never anonymous.** `/v1/inbound/**` is on `jwt.public-paths` because BACEN holds no PlatinumCoin token — a real participant presents mTLS + an ICP-Brasil certificate, a whole trust domain away from our HS256 tokens. But the route **credits money**, so it is guarded by the shared `SPI_WEBHOOK_TOKEN` (`{{spiWebhookToken}}`), compared constant-time before anything else runs: without it, any process reaching port 8086 could mint spendable balance (threat model, boundary B4).

Normally you trigger this through **mock-bacen-spi › Simulate an inbound Pix**; the requests here exist to poke the two properties that flow hides — the **dedupe** and the **guard**. Run the simulate request first: it fills `{{inboundEndToEndId}}`.

exec: pm.test('200 OK — a redelivery is a success, not an error', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));

request.description:
What BACEN does when it never got an answer: present the **same payment again**. Run **mock-bacen-spi › Simulate an inbound Pix to bob** first, then this — and check bob's balance before and after (**ledger-service › Balance**). It does not move.

`200 {outcome:"ALREADY_PROCESSED"}`, not an error: the rail asked "did you accept this payment?", and to one already credited the truthful answer is still yes. An error here would have BACEN re-presenting a payment that *was* delivered.

**How it is deduped.** The transaction id is `in-<endToEndId>`, so the item's partition key embeds the rail's own id and `attribute_not_exists(pk)` **is** the dedupe — strongly consistent, atomic, correct under concurrent redelivery. Querying the `E2E#` GSI instead would be a read-then-check over an *eventually consistent* index: two simultaneous deliveries could both read "absent" and both credit.

The same determinism makes the ledger posting idempotent, which is why the credit runs **before** the conditional record rather than after a claim — a crash in between replays harmlessly, whereas claiming first would mark a payment handled whose money never arrived.

item.name: Forged webhook — no token (401, nothing credited)

exec: pm.test('the refusal does not echo the secret back', () =>

request.description:
The boundary that stands between "JWT-exempt" and "anonymous" (threat model **B4**). No `X-Webhook-Token`, a fresh `endToEndId` and an absurd amount — `401 WEBHOOK_UNAUTHORIZED`, and **nothing happens**: no directory lookup, no ledger posting, no transaction. Check bob's balance to confirm.

The check is the *first* thing the use case does, deliberately — so a forged call cannot cost anything, nor reveal by side effect whether the key it named exists. The refusal never echoes the configured token back, and neither token is ever logged (ADR-0012: the log-the-values licence stops at secrets).

Try it with a **wrong** token too, and with one that merely starts correctly: the comparison is equality and constant-time, so a correct prefix buys nothing — not even timing information.
Liveness/readiness for the compose healthcheck. Public — `/actuator/**` is on the JWT allow-list.

item.name: notification-service
item.description:
Real-time push (port 8087). One **SSE** connection per authenticated customer, fed from `notification-queue` — the last hop of the receive flow, and the honest ending to a `202 Accepted`.

**Postman is the wrong tool for the happy path, and that is worth knowing.** An SSE response never finishes: the server holds it open and writes frames as payments happen. Postman's runner waits for a response that completes, so the stream card below will simply spin until you cancel it. Use `curl -N` or the **API explorer** (`tools/api-explorer/index.html`), which reads the stream incrementally and renders each frame. What Postman *is* good for here is the auth surface — the two 401 cards below complete instantly and assert the real contract.

**Why SSE and not WebSocket:** notifications are one-directional server→client, so SSE is plain HTTP with no upgrade, no framing, no client library — and the browser's native `EventSource` reconnects on its own. WebSocket would buy a channel back to the server this feature has no use for.

**Best-effort by design:** a missed push costs a refresh, never correctness — every outcome stays queryable on `GET /payments/{transactionId}`.

**What a frame carries (step 39).** Every `data:` line is the SAME seven fields, whatever the event: `{transactionId, type, status, amount, counterpart, timestamp, failureReason}` — a strict subset of the `Payment` schema `GET /v1/payments/{transactionId}` answers, so a client parses the push and the poll with one parser and one vocabulary (`SETTLED`, `REVERSED`; an *arrival* is `SETTLED` too, because the direction lives in `type`). `amount` is already a decimal string — integer cents are formatted at this edge and nowhere earlier — and `counterpart` is a display value (the payee's key on a send, the payer's name on an arrival), never an internal account id. Routing: `PixSettled`/`PixReversed` reach the **payer**, `PixReceived` the **payee**.

**To watch it as a customer would**, open `tools/api-explorer/index.html` → the **Phone** tab: same endpoint, same bytes, rendered as a phone's lock screen.

item.name: My notification stream (SSE — long-lived, will not "finish")

exec: // These only run if the stream ever completes (i.e. after the 30-minute server-side timeout,
// or when you cancel). They are here so the contract is stated, not because Postman is the
// right client for a stream — see the folder description.

request.description:
Opens **your** stream. Log in first (auth-service folder) — the account comes from the JWT `accountId` claim and there is no path, query or body parameter naming an account, so "stream someone else's payments" is not a request this API can express. That is the read-side of Domain Safety Rule #1: stronger than an ownership check, because nothing is left to check.

What arrives on the wire:

```
:connected sub-9f3a…        ← handshake, an SSE comment (every client ignores it for free)
:ping                       ← every 25s, so proxies never reclaim an idle stream
event:PixReceived           ← the event type, in the SSE frame's OWN field
id:evt-1c8b…                ← the eventId, so a reconnect can resume via Last-Event-ID
data:{"txId":"…","amountCents":1234,"status":"RECEIVED_SETTLED", …}
```

To make an event appear: send an external Pix (payment-service folder) and watch for `PixSettled`, or trigger an inbound one with **mock-bacen-spi → Simulate an inbound Pix to bob** and watch for `PixReceived`. Routing is one sentence: *an outcome of a send belongs to the payer, an arrival belongs to the payee* — so log in as the right user or nothing will arrive (and that is correct behaviour, not a failure).

Step 38 pushes the raw event payload; **step 39** standardizes `data` on the same external status vocabulary `GET /payments/{transactionId}` uses, so clients parse one shape everywhere.

**The frame you will see** (step 39):

```
event:PixSettled
id:evt-6f1a…
data:{"transactionId":"tx-8f2c","type":"PixSettled","status":"SETTLED","amount":"987.00","counterpart":"bob@otherbank.com","timestamp":"2026-08-20T10:15:00Z","failureReason":null}
```

Lines starting with `:` are comments — `:connected …` on open and `:ping` every 25s — which every SSE client ignores for free.

exec: pm.test('the shared RFC 7807 contract, not a bespoke one', () => {

request.description:
The stream is **not** on the JWT allow-list. Step 05 reserved a hook there for the SSE handshake's awkwardness, and step 38 deliberately did not spend it — see the next card for why that matters.

Completes instantly with the same `401 problem+json` every other protected route returns, because it is refused by the same common-lib filter.

exec: pm.test('the query-parameter path is a convenience, not a second, weaker verifier', () =>

request.description:
**The SSE handshake nuance, and its guard rail.** A browser's native `EventSource` cannot set request headers — there is no API for it — so a stream that only accepts `Authorization` is a stream no `EventSource` can open. notification-service therefore accepts `?access_token=` on this one path.

It is a convenience, **not a hole**, and this card is the proof: `SseTokenHandshakeFilter` merely rewrites the parameter into an `Authorization` header just before common-lib's `JwtAuthFilter` runs, so a bad token is refused by exactly the same code with exactly the same body, whichever way it was presented. The route is never made public, and an explicit header always wins over the parameter.

Remove `TAMPERED` and the stream opens (and hangs — see the folder description). The cost accepted here: a token in a URL lands in access logs, `Referer` and browser history. Bounded by being a 15-minute token, on one path, in a sandbox; production would mint a single-use stream ticket instead.
Liveness/readiness for the compose healthcheck. Public — `/actuator/**` is on the JWT allow-list.

item.name: ledger-service
item.description: The ledger — port 8085, the ONLY writer of `pix_ledger` (ADR-0006). Steps 13-14 ship both halves: a **strongly consistent** balance read (`ConsistentRead=true`, because the ledger must read its own writes — a stale balance would show money that is already spent). Every request here needs a token: `/internal/**` is deliberately not public, and this service has no `/v1` surface at all, because no end user talks to the ledger. See services/ledger-service/README.md.

exec: // Two representations of ONE number: decimal string for humans, integer cents for
// the services that do arithmetic on it. They must never disagree.
// version is the posting counter — an audit aid, never a lock (ARCHITECTURE §6.3).
pm.test('untouched account is at version 0', () => pm.expect(body.version).to.eql(0));

request.description: Balance of one ledger account, read with `ConsistentRead=true`. Returns `{accountId, balance, balanceCents, version}` — `balance` is a decimal BRL string for the human, `balanceCents` the same amount as an integer for internal callers (payment-service, step 21). Seeded by step 12 at R$ 10,000.00. Not account-scoped on purpose: this is an internal seam, so alice's token may read bob's balance (`acc-002`) — the "debited account comes from the JWT" rule binds the money-moving endpoint in payment-service, and nothing here moves money.

exec: // Negative by construction: it is the debit counterpart of every seeded balance.

request.description: `ACCOUNT#SEED` is the double-entry counterpart of the whole money supply, so its balance is **negative by construction** (-R$ 20,000.00). With acc-001, acc-002 and `SPI_CLEARING` (at 0), Σ over every account is **zero** — the conservation invariant step 15 asserts under a concurrent debit storm. System accounts are exempt from the no-negative-balance guard on WRITES, never from being read. Swap `SEED` for `SPI_CLEARING` in the path to see the clearing account at rest.

exec: // NOT a balance of zero: in a ledger 'no such account' and 'no money' are opposite facts.
pm.test('no balance is returned at all', () => pm.expect(body.balanceCents).to.be.undefined);

request.description: An account with no BALANCE item ⇒ 404 problem+json (`code: LEDGER_ACCOUNT_NOT_FOUND`), never a balance of zero — the two are opposite facts in a ledger and must not look alike on the wire. Drop the `Authorization` header to see the other failure mode: 401 (`code: UNAUTHORIZED`), because `/internal/**` is not public here either.

exec: // The ledger's idempotency key is the txId in the BODY, not an Idempotency-Key
// header: it is the identity of the posting itself, shared by every caller that
// retries it. Generated once here and kept in a collection variable so the next two
// requests can replay and conflict with THIS posting.
pm.test('this call committed the posting', () => pm.expect(body.replayed).to.eql(false));
// postedAt is the instant embedded in both ENTRY sort keys — keep it to compare
// against the replay below, which must return THIS instant, not its own.

request.description:
The atomic double-entry posting: **one** `TransactWriteItems` of five items — debit balance (condition `balanceCents >= :amount`), credit balance, the two immutable ENTRY legs, and the `TX#<txId>/POSTING` idempotency guard. All or nothing: no state exists in which the debit landed without its credit.

Money on the wire is **integer cents** (`amountCents`); the response echoes both `amount` ("125.50", for you) and `amountCents` (for the services that do arithmetic). Run "Balance (alice)" afterwards: 10000.00 → 9874.50, while bob gains exactly the same — Σ over every account is unchanged, because a posting *moves* money.

item.name: Posting — replay the same txId (200, replayed)

exec: pm.test('200 OK — a replay is a success, not an error', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
// The answer describes when the money MOVED, not when this retry arrived.

request.description:
Byte-identical to the previous request — the retry a caller makes when a response is lost. Answer: **200 with `replayed: true`**, and alice's balance does *not* move a second time (check it).

This works because the guard item is keyed on the `txId` **alone**. Keying it on the entry (`ENTRY#<timestamp>#<txId>`) would not: the retry arrives at a new instant, so the key would differ, `attribute_not_exists` would pass, and the payer would be debited twice.

Both outcomes are 200 on purpose. An API that answered differently would train callers to treat a retry as a failure and mint a *new* txId — the one reaction that actually double-spends.

The same `txId` for a different amount. The ledger refuses instead of guessing: answering "already done" would silently swallow this payment, and posting it would double-spend the first one. 409 is the only answer that loses nothing — mint a new `txId` for a new intent.

(`description` is deliberately *not* part of that comparison: a label is not money, so a retry that regenerated its text still replays.)

R$ 999,999.99 out of an account holding R$ 10,000.00 ⇒ **422 INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS**, and — the part that matters — **nothing at all is written**: no balance moved, no entry appended, no guard item left behind. Run "Balance (alice)" to confirm.

That is guaranteed by *where* the check lives: `balanceCents >= :amount` is a condition **inside** the transaction, evaluated by DynamoDB as part of the debit. Reading the balance first and deciding in Java would be the same code with a race in it.

Other refusals worth trying by hand: both legs on one account ⇒ 422 `INVALID_POSTING`; an unknown `creditAccount` ⇒ 404 `LEDGER_ACCOUNT_NOT_FOUND` (an upsert would otherwise have *created* the account); `"amountCents": 0` ⇒ 400 `VALIDATION_ERROR`; no `Authorization` header ⇒ 401.

exec: // Newest first: timestamps are non-increasing down the page (lexicographic == chronological).
// Each entry ships both money representations of ONE signed number.
// nextCursor is opaque: echo it back to fetch the following page (null ⇒ last page).

request.description:
One page of acc-001's statement, **newest first**. The ordering is free: the sort key is `ENTRY#<isoTimestamp>#<txId>`, so `Query begins_with(sk,"ENTRY#")` with `ScanIndexForward=false` is already reverse-chronological — no sort anywhere.

Pagination is DynamoDB-native, not offset-based: `nextCursor` is the base64 of the query's `LastEvaluatedKey`, **opaque** to you. To fetch the next page, enable the `cursor` query param and paste `nextCursor` into it (the test script also stashes it in `{{ledgerNextCursor}}`). `nextCursor: null` means you have reached the end of the history.

`limit` is clamped by the service (default 20, max 100). Each entry carries both `amount` ("-125.50", signed decimal string for you) and `amountCents` (the signed integer for callers that do arithmetic). Post a few times with the "Posting" request first to grow the history past one page.

A cursor that does not decode ⇒ **400 INVALID_CURSOR**. The same 400 answers a *well-formed* cursor that names a **different account**: the token embeds the partition key (`ACCOUNT#<id>`), so editing it to page someone else's history hands the ledger a key that does not match the path — refused, never silently paging the other account.
Actuator health — the contract compose healthchecks rely on. Expect {"status":"UP"}.

item.name: fraud-service
item.description: Synchronous fraud scoring — port 8083. Backed by Redis (velocity counters; ADR-0008, the ElastiCache stand-in). POST /internal/fraud/score (step 24) scores a transfer with cheap in-path rules under a p99 < 150ms budget; payment-service calls it with the 200ms timeout + fail-open flag in step 25. See services/fraud-service/README.md.

exec: pm.test('score and reasons are present', () => { pm.expect(body.score).to.be.a('number'); pm.expect(body.reasons).to.be.an('array'); });

request.description:
Rule-based in-path score (step 24) → `{decision, score, reasons[]}` under a p99 < 150ms budget. Four cheap rules read pre-computed Redis features (no model, no DB): HIGH_AMOUNT (single value), VELOCITY_COUNT/VELOCITY_AMOUNT (rolling INCR/EXPIRE windows), NEW_PAYEE (persistent SADD set) and ODD_HOURS (São Paulo overnight window). A first small daytime transfer scores only NEW_PAYEE (15) → APPROVE.

**Try DENY:** raise `amountCents` above R$5,000 (e.g. 5000000) — HIGH_AMOUNT alone (weight 70) hits the deny band. **Try REVIEW:** fire this request 5+ times in a minute with the same `accountId` — VELOCITY_COUNT crosses the threshold.

`accountId` is a body field here (not the JWT) because this is an internal service-to-service seam: payment-service, which already took the account from *its* token (Domain Safety Rule #1), forwards it as data. `/internal/**` is authenticated, so a Bearer token is still required.
Actuator health — the contract compose healthchecks rely on. Expect {"status":"UP"}.

item.name: mock-bacen-spi
item.description: BACEN's **SPI** (the instant-payment rail) and **DICT** (key directory), stubbed — port 9090. The one component whose job is to *misbehave on demand*: latency, failure and timeout are armable at runtime (`POST /admin/config`), which is what makes Sprint 7's retries, DLQ and reconciliation testable at all. **No token on any request here**: BACEN is outside PlatinumCoin's trust domain (a real participant presents mTLS + an ICP-Brasil certificate), so `jwt.public-paths` is `/**`. Settlements are held in memory — restarting the container wipes BACEN's memory, which is a drill, not a defect. See services/mock-bacen-spi/README.md.

request.description:
Settle one Pix over the rail. **Idempotent by `endToEndId`** — the first terminal outcome for an id wins forever and a replay is byte-for-byte the original answer, `recordedAt` included. That indistinguishability is what makes retrying after a timeout *safe* rather than merely likely to work: the caller needs no special case for "maybe it already happened".

Send this request twice and compare `recordedAt` — it does not move. Money is integer cents on the wire (`amountCents`), never a decimal string. A creditor key no participant holds ⇒ `422 SPI_REJECTED` (permanent — step 33 reverses on it); with `failureRate` armed ⇒ `503 SPI_UNAVAILABLE` (transient — **nothing recorded**, so the same id can still settle).

item.name: Settle a Pix — replay the same endToEndId (one settlement)

exec: pm.test('replays the FIRST settlement, not a second one', () => pm.expect(body.recordedAt).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('spiRecordedAt')));

request.description:
Run *Settle a Pix* first, then this: same `endToEndId`, and the answer carries the original `recordedAt`. One settlement, not two — the third layer of the platform's idempotency (ADR-0002: API key → ledger `txId` → SPI `endToEndId`), and the layer that makes step 32's retry loop safe.

Try changing `amountCents` here: the **recorded** amount is replayed and the mismatch is logged loudly. An `endToEndId` identifies one transfer; a second amount is not a correction.

exec: pm.test('200 OK — even for an id the SPI never saw', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
pm.test('carries one of the three answers', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().status).to.be.oneOf(['SETTLED','FAILED','UNKNOWN']));

request.description:
What became of an `endToEndId` — the lookup reconciliation lives on (ADR-0003), and the one a caller must make **before** retrying a settlement that timed out (step 32).

**Always `200`, never `404`.** "I have never heard of this id" is an answer the caller has to act on, and a `404` would be indistinguishable from a typo in the URL — so absence is reported in the body as `UNKNOWN`, with no amount (reporting `0` for a transfer the SPI never saw would be a lie reconciliation might act on). Edit the id in the path to `E-never-sent` to see it.

Break the rail **while the stack is running** — the drills this exists for are sequences, not states ("send a payment, *then* break BACEN, watch the retries, un-break it"), and restarting a container between those steps would reset the SPI's memory of every settlement.

**Partial by design:** an absent field is left unchanged, so this arms one knob without resetting a latency set a moment earlier. Out-of-range values (a "probability" above 1, a latency beyond the real SPI's 10s SLA) are refused with `400 VALIDATION_ERROR` rather than clamped silently — a drill must not pass against a fiction. `0.0`/`1.0` are exact, never probabilistic.

The **send-reachable reversal trigger** (step 35). Unlike `failureRate` (a *transient* 503 that records nothing) or an unknown creditor key (refused already at *send* time), this refuses a **DICT-known** key at *settlement* — so a real external Pix to `bob@otherbank.com` debits to clearing, then settlement gets `422 SETTLEMENT_REJECTED_BY_ADMIN`, and step 33's compensating reversal fires against the compose stack.

Drill: arm this, send an external Pix to `bob@otherbank.com` (*Send Pix*), then watch `GET /payments/{id}` reach `REVERSED` and the payer's balance restored. Clear it with `{"rejectKeys": []}`. Partial like every knob: an absent `rejectKeys` leaves the list unchanged.

exec: pm.test('rail healthy again', () => { const b = pm.response.json(); pm.expect(b.failureRate).to.eql(0.0); pm.expect(b.timeoutRate).to.eql(0.0); pm.expect(b.rejectKeys).to.eql([]); });

request.description:
Put the rail back to the compose defaults, clearing every drill (latency, failure, timeout **and** the reject list). Run this after any drill — the dial is global mutable state and survives until changed or the container restarts.

`timeoutRate` is the interesting knob to try instead: a rolled timeout **settles and then hangs** past the caller's timeout, manufacturing the nastiest state in distributed payments — the money moved and the caller believes it did not. That is the case *Settlement status* exists to reveal.

What is armed right now, including the read-only `timeoutHangMs` — so a confusing run can be explained instead of guessed at. `timeoutHangMs` is boot-time configuration: a value lowerable mid-drill would turn a "timeout" into a slow success.

exec: pm.test('names the holding participant', () => { const b = pm.response.json(); pm.expect(b.ispb).to.eql('99999999'); pm.expect(b.keyType).to.eql('EMAIL'); });

request.description:
Which participant holds a Pix key → `{key, keyType, ispb, participant}`. This is what account-service calls for any key it does not hold locally (step 30), and the ISPB it surfaces as `externalBank`.

**Deliberately outside the failure injection:** this lookup sits on the *synchronous* send path with the payer waiting on it (p99 < 2s), while settlement is the asynchronous half nobody waits for — slowing the directory would blow the send SLO and prove nothing about settlement resilience. Seeded keys: `bob@otherbank.com`, `carol@otherbank.com` (ISPB 99999999), `+5511977776666`, `98765432100` (ISPB 88888888). Anything else ⇒ `404 DICT_KEY_NOT_FOUND`.

No participant holds this key — the **only** case in which a payer may be told the key does not exist. Every other outcome of this call (connection refused, timeout, `5xx`) means "we could not ask", which account-service refuses to translate into "does not exist": it answers `503 DIRECTORY_UNAVAILABLE` instead.

request.description:
**The trigger that makes money arrive** (step 37) — the one direction where this stub is the *caller*: it mints an `endToEndId` and presents the payment to settlement-service's webhook (`POST :8086/v1/inbound/pix`, `X-Webhook-Token`), retrying like a real rail.

Receiving is the **mirror** of sending: an outbound send debits the payer and credits `SPI_CLEARING`; this debits `SPI_CLEARING` and credits bob (`entryType=PIX_IN`). Same double entry, opposite direction — Σ balances still moves by exactly the amount received and no leg dangles.

Register `bob@platinum.com` first (**account-service › Register Pix key**): the payee is whatever *our* directory says the key belongs to, never something the caller names — the inbound mirror of Domain Safety Rule #1 (note the body has no account field at all).

`amount` is a decimal string here because a **human** types it; the webhook one hop later carries integer `amountCents`, because a machine-to-machine rail edge has no reader to format for. The response's `endToEndId` is saved to `{{inboundEndToEndId}}` so the next request can re-present it.

A key nobody here answers for ⇒ `422 INBOUND_REFUSED` (the participant answered `422 KEY_NOT_FOUND`) — a real rail bounces the payment back to the payer's PSP rather than re-presenting it forever.
Actuator health — the contract compose healthchecks rely on. Expect {"status":"UP"}.
